paper_title: WeightCode: Installing New Capabilities into Neural Networks via Weight-Space Programming

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Neural networks encode learned capabilities in their weights, yet extending those capabilities with explicit task knowledge remains a fundamental challenge. Here we show that Weight-Space Programming (WSP), in which executable programs read, construct or modify a network's weights directly, can install new capabilities within trained neural networks. WeightCode, a WSP framework, uses a frozen language model to write executable weight programs that install new computations into trained neural networks using task knowledge and their existing weights, without gradient-based training. Once installed, the new capabilities run independently of the language model. Given a grammar or eight demonstrations, weight programs enable previously unseen command compositions (0% to 99.8% exact match) and a new pickup action (0% to 98.4% success), while preserving the original command and navigation capabilities. On ImageNet, four weight programs achieve net gains of 8.84-17.62 points while preserving clean accuracy, outperforming the best of eight fine-tuning methods under matched examples, checks, and retention constraints. In a Vision Transformer, causal interventions show that installed noise-correction gates drive robustness gains, while their selective activation preserves clean accuracy. Rerun on five independently trained Vision Transformers without further language model calls, ten weight programs retain 83-110% of their source-network gains on average, whereas copying their fixed weight edits yields negligible gains. Six programs written for an already edited network add 5.23-14.50 points of contrast robustness while retaining the previously installed noise gain. Together, these results establish WSP as a new route to acquiring and accumulating capabilities in trained neural networks through reusable weight programs.

Six programs written for an already edited network add 5.2314.50 points of contrast robustness while retaining the previously installed noise gain. Together, these results establish WSP as new route to acquiring and accumulating capabilities in trained neural networks through reusable weight programs. 1. Introduction Learning capability during training and installing one into an already trained neural network are distinct problems. The latter requires translating task knowledge into new computations while preserving previously acquired capabilities. Unlike software, whose functionality can be extended through executable instructions, neural networks encode learned computations in distributed weights. Can executable programs directly construct new capabilities within these weights, and can subsequent programs build upon those already installed? Following [1, 2], we call this paradigm Weight-Space Programming (WSP): executable programs read, construct or modify the weights of neural network directly. Its artifact, the executable weight program, retains how networkspecific update is constructed, rather than only the numerical weight changes it produces. Fine-tuning [3, 4], model editing [5, 6], and test-time adaptation [7, 8] provide established ways to update trained networks. Meanwhile, large language models (LLMs) can generate and refine executable programs through evaluation feedback [9, 10] and have recently been shown to inspect and modify neural weights directly [1]. Four fundamental questions define the scope of WSP: Installation. Can weight program install new capability into trained network while preserving previously acquired capabilities? Mechanism. What computation does weight program install, and how does it produce the new capability? Reuse. Can the same weight program be rerun without the LLM to construct effective edits in independently trained networks? Succession. Can new weight program extend an already edited network while preserving capabilities installed by earlier programs? Here we introduce WeightCode, WSP framework in which frozen LLM writes executable weight programs that install, reuse and accumulate capabilities in trained neural networks (Fig. 1a). weight program reads the networks weights and task knowledge I, such as rule, demonstrations, or labeled examples, and constructs updated weights = p(W, I). Evaluation feedback selects programs that improve the new capability while preserving existing behavior. The updated network executes the installed computation within its original architecture, without the LLM at inference. The retained program can be rerun on compatible networks to construct network-specific edits. New programs can then extend networks already modified by earlier programs. Across language, navigation, and visual recognition, weight programs transform rules, demonstrations, and labeled examples into new capabilities (Fig. 1b, Fig. 2). On SCAN, program modifies 257 weights to raise exact match on previously unseen command compositions from 0.0% to 99.8%; on BabyAI, eight demonstrations enable new pickup action with 98.4% success. On ImageNet, four weight programs achieve 8.8417.62 points of net gain under corruption while preserving clean accuracy, outperforming eight fine-tuning methods under matched examples, checks, and retention constraints. Causal interventions reveal how installed noise-correction gates produce robustness gains while their selective activation preserves clean accuracy  (Fig. 3)  . Rerun on five independently trained Vision Transformers, ten weight programs retain 83110% of their source-network gains on average, whereas copying fixed weight edits yields negligible gains (Fig. 1c, Fig. 4). Six second-round programs written for an already edited network add contrast robustness while retaining the previously installed noise robustness (Fig. 1d, Fig. 5). To2 gether, these findings establish WSP as new paradigm for extending trained neural networks: capabilities can be programmed into existing weights, reconstructed across independently trained networks, and progressively expanded through successive weight programs. 2. Related work Existing approaches to modifying trained networks differ in how they construct, represent and reuse changes to model parameters. Learning and retaining capabilities. Fine-tuning adds capability by optimizing parameters on labeled data, in full or through parameter-efficient modules [3, 11], and regularized transfer keeps the new parameters close to the old ones [12]. Sequential training overwrites earlier capabilities [13, 14], and continual learning limits this forgetting by regularizing parameters [15] or outputs [4], or by replaying stored examples [16]. Test-time adaptation adjusts network to new input condition from unlabeled inputs, by re-estimating normalization statistics [7], minimizing prediction entropy [8, 17] or training on self-supervised task [18]. Targeted and lifelong model editing. Model editing changes trained networks behavior on target inputs while preserving it elsewhere: by gradient steps on network trained to be editable [19], by learned editor networks [20], or by closed-form rewrites of layers viewed as associative memories [5, 6, 21, 22]. Lifelong editing applies edits in sequence, for example by storing each one in discrete keyvalue codebook attached to layer [23]. Composing and transferring weight changes. Task arithmetic adds and subtracts the weight differences of finetuned models [24], and model merging resolves the interference between such differences when it combines them [25]. Both act on models that share pretrained starting point, and merging independently trained networks first aligns their units by permutation [26]. These methods operate on learned parameter differences, whose transfer and combination depend on the relationship between model parameterizations. Program discovery and weight-space methods. Language models have been used to discover executable algorithms, reward functions, policies, skills and training objectives [9, 10, 2730], and symbolic search and meta-learning discover optimizers [31, 32]. Separately, work on hypernetworks, weight-space learning and program-to-network compilation has established several ways to construct or analyze neural computation through weights [3339]. In Weight-Space Programming. concurrent work, Takehi et al. [1] show that frontier LLM can read the weights of small networks, write networks from zero weights and edit trained networks, and Li et al. [2] have an LLM write an editor that refits the output weights or coefficients of trained predictors from measured feedback. These studies show that language models can carry out WSP, inspecting and modifying neural weights directly. WeightCode shows that the weight programs that construct such updates, retained after the update, can be rerun on independently trained networks and extended by subsequent programs, so that the construction procedure itself becomes reusable object. 3. WeightCode WeightCode realizes WSP by separating the construction of an update from its execution: frozen LLM writes an executable weight program, and the program computes network-specific weight changes (Fig. 1a). 3.1. Installing capability with program Weight programs. weight program is code that takes trained networks weights and task knowledge I, what is known about new capability, and returns new weights: = p(W, I), = p(W, I) W. (1) is the weight edit of one run. It depends on the network the program reads as well as on the program, so the same program run on another network computes another edit. program may read every weight, run the networks forward pass on inputs and read I. The updated network keeps its architecture and forward code, with only its weights changed, and runs on its own at inference. The experiments impose additional implementation constraints, including sandboxed execution and maximum edit size of 20% of the networks weights (Sec. A.1). What program writes. In WeightCode, the form of the update is chosen for each capability and each network. The LLM proposes candidate computations and weight modifications from the networks weights, its activations and the task knowledge, and evaluation feedback determines which candidate is kept. The programs reported here connect the new capability to computation the network already performs (Tab. 9). The Gaussian-noise program for the ViTLite, for example, measures how noise shifts the patch tokens, finds MLP units that are nearly idle on clean images, and rewrites two of them in each of three blocks as gates that open when token moves along the noise direction and then subtract the measured shift (Fig. 3a). Other programs reuse the networks own representations, such as the embeddings of known primitives on SCAN or of known instruction in the BabyAI policy. Writing and checking. The LLM writes the program in one session, in Python kernel that holds , the forward pass and I. Keeping existing behavior. Preservation is evaluated on task-specific reference conditions: clean-image accuracy for the image classifiers, the previously supported commands or mission for the sequence and navigation tasks, and the previously installed conditions for successive updates. Keeping these is part of how program is chosen. The kept program is the checked candidate with the highest Snew + Sold among those with Sold 20, loss of at most 0.5% of 4,000 clean check images (the retention rule). On SCAN the bound is 5 of 1,000 old commands and on BabyAI 3 of 500 old episodes. If no candidate qualifies, the network is left unchanged. The bound is applied on the check split, and the reference conditions are measured on held-out inputs (Sec. 3.3). Feedback without gradients. Weight programs construct updates through direct computations on weights, activations and forward passes, namely weight and activation statistics, SVD and PCA, label-free closed-form fits and single-unit ablations, rather than by optimizing an objective on the networks outputs. Labeled feedback evaluates and selects candidate programs rather than fitting their values: singleround session scores at most 8 candidate edits against the labeled examples and receives 8 checks, as each fine-tuning method tries 8 configurations and receives the same checks. Label-scored work that changes no weight, and selection inside programs own run, are counted separately from this cap (Sec. A.1). An automatic audit and reading of the kept programs check these rules; three exploratory sessions that use finite differences are reported separately (Sec. A.11), and Sec. A.1 lists what the protocol admits. 3.2. Rerunning and extending programs Programs as reusable construction procedures. An executable weight program retains the procedure that constructed an update: how the network is measured, how units or directions are selected and what is written into them. Run on another compatible network, the same program remeasures that network and constructs new edit in its weight coordinates. This matters for independently trained networks, which may implement related functions in different coordinates [26], so that numerical edit computed on one network need not apply to another. Copying, rerunning and successive updates. Three operations act on program p1 kept for network W0 and task knowledge I1, which produces W1 = p1(W0, I1). Copying adds the edit W1 W0 unchanged to another network. Rerunning executes the code of p1 unchanged and without another LLM session, while the program inspects the target network and uses that networks own task examples, so each rerun computes an edit from that networks weights and data. successive update asks the LLM for new program p2 for the edited network W1, which produces W2 = p2(W1, I2). This new program is constructed with the edited network, the code of p1, labeled examples of the new condition and checks that also report every earlier condition, under the retention rule for each, so that the update can account for the computations installed earlier. We rerun programs on independently trained networks of the architecture they were written for, and write second programs for edited networks. 3.3. Experimental protocol Networks. Weight programs install computations that can be tested part by part Weight programs produce identifiable internal computations whose causal contributions to the new behavior can be tested directly (Fig. 3; Tab. 9 describes every program and marks those tested by intervention; selection split). The noise program writes conditional correction into existing units. The installed correction detects shift in the networks internal representations and subtracts measured offset selectively from the affected tokens. By examining the supplied images and the networks activations, the LLM finds that the corruption mainly shifts the patch tokens in the early residual stream, and builds the correction on that shift; untold, it also infers additive white Gaussian pixel noise of standard deviation about 25/255 (the generating value is 0.10). Discussion The central finding is that trained neural network can be extended by an executable construction procedure whose output becomes part of the networks own computation. The updated network performs the new capability on its own, while the program retains the procedure that built it from existing computation. Capability installation therefore has an explicit implementation that can be tested by intervention and recomputed by rerunning the program. This separates the reusable specification of capability from the network-specific weight values that implement it. These results reveal mechanism of capability acquisition in which task knowledge is translated into new computation by recruiting and reorganizing operations already represented within trained network. Rules, examples and checks specify the desired behavior, while the networks weights and activations inform how it can be implemented: programs reconnect existing representations, recruit learned operations or add corrections for particular inputs. In the noise-gating programs, preservation is built into the computation itself, in addition to the retention rule that selects them: the correction activates mainly on affected inputs and leaves clean representations nearly unchanged, and causal interventions separate the two roles, with the installed computation producing the robustness gain and its selective activation protecting clean accuracy. The source of new capability and the reason the measured existing behavior is kept can thus be examined directly and used to inform the design of later programs. Reusability changes what can be retained after an update: not only the modified network, but also an executable description of how the modification was constructed. Rerun on another network, that description recomputes an edit for the networks own weights; written for an edited network, new program can account for what earlier programs installed. As capabilities accumulate, previously installed 10 computations become part of the foundation that later updates can use and preserve, and these properties motivate reusable program libraries and longer sequences of capability updates, each retained together with its checks. Natural next steps are programs that construct representations network does not yet have (Sec. A.10) and programs that extend foundation models, including LLMs, with new procedures or behaviors after deployment. More broadly, WSP provides foundation for self-directed capability extension, in which proposed changes to networks computation are evaluated independently, retained and built upon through further weight programs, each remaining code that can be read and tested. Training establishes the initial computation of neural network. Executable weight programs offer complementary route: task knowledge becomes part of the networks own computation while its measured existing behavior is kept, and each update is retained as procedure that can be inspected, rerun and extended. Weight-Space Programming thereby opens path to cumulative capability acquisition, in which new computations are installed, reused and progressively extended within trained neural networks.
